open: Post-fix the desk places 13187 buy orders for 492 fills, a 3.7% conversion. That asymmetry between placed and filled is unexplained and may be a second defect in its quoting.
caveats: Two seeds.
Detected only because the metaorder defect prompted a reject-rate audit broken out by role, which had not been done in 190 experiments.

title: Fill loss is a clean sublinear function of admitted-throughput deficit
design: Swept metaorder_trader orders_per_day over 2000, 3000, 4500, 6000, 8000, 12000 on def_control.json, seed 91, 8h, holding the seed fixed so the dose varies by design rather than by draw. Dose = 1 - admitted_budgeted/admitted_control. Response = filled-quantity loss. Post the INVALID_QTY fix (4981384), pre the round-trip funding fix (f37b702).
finding: Across a 0 to 64% dose range the relationship is close to linear with slope 0.836 and R2 0.989, and the intercept is within a percentage point of zero. Denying the desk a tenth of its admitted requests costs it about 8.4% of executed quantity. Parent-count loss tracks quantity loss at every point, confirming the throughput mechanism from E-192 and E-194.
methodological_finding: This resolves what three rounds of per-seed ratios could not. Ratios taken at one cap ranged from 0.16 to 2.19 and were read as seed disagreement; they were an unstable estimator sampling one noisy point of this line. Sweeping the dose within a fixed seed turns the same underlying relationship into a tight fit. The intercept is the check the ratio form could never provide: a nonzero intercept would have meant the dose variable was contaminated.
caveats: One seed. E-197 replicates on seeds 91-92.
Ran on the population that lacked a working round-trip desk (f37b702), so the slope describes a market missing its inventory mean-reversion mechanism. E-197 re-runs against the corrected population.
Sublinearity is measured, not explained. The slope below one may be saturation at high dose rather than a uniform property; the two highest-dose points sit furthest below the line.
next: E-197: same sweep on the corrected population, seeds 91 and 92, with a 1500 cap added to extend the dose range.

title: Restoring the round-trip desk halves maker inventory
design: Compared maker_state inventory series across commit f37b702 on def_control.json, seeds 91-92, 8h, 5 spot makers per run. The desk's stated purpose is to return maker inventory through symmetric round trips, so the directional prediction was fixed by its design before measuring.
finding: Mean absolute maker inventory falls 53% on seed 91 and 21% on seed 92, standard deviation falls on both, and mean inventory moves toward zero on both. The desk delivers the inventory mean reversion it was added for, which the population has been missing.
correction: Without the desk, makers ran systematically short (-124 and -109), not long as guessed when the defect was found. The direction was observable in maker_state throughout and did not need to be guessed.
caveats: Two seeds, five makers, one configuration.
Adding roughly 1000 symmetric fills changes more than inventory; the inventory effect is the pre-specified prediction, but other differences between these runs are not controlled.
Effect size differs a lot between seeds (53% against 21%).
open: The desk converts only 3.7% of placed orders into fills because cross() sends IOC at the touch rather than through it, so the touch has moved by arrival. Metaorder children, which price through the touch with a slippage allowance, convert 27-43%. A stronger desk would likely show a larger effect.

title: Sub-minimum orders were pure waste: removing 44k requests per run leaves the market identical
design: A/B of commit 9331329 on def_control.json, seed 91, 8h. Compared accepted orders, fills and rejects per role.
finding: Rejects go to zero while accepted orders and fills are identical to the unit. The orders removed could never have traded, so the fix is pure waste removal with no behavioural change and determinism preserved.
implication: Population request totals in this campaign carried roughly 44k guaranteed-invalid requests per 8h run. Any rate-limit measurement taken over population totals rather than per-role admitted counts was inflated by that amount. Per-role measurements of metaorder_trader, which is what E-195 and E-197 use, are unaffected.
open: carry_arb still converts only 6.8% of accepted orders into fills, and round_trip 7.4%. Both send IOC at the touch rather than through it, so the touch has moved by arrival. This is a design property, not a rejection, but it means both desks are much weaker than their request counts suggest.

title: The dose response is concave, not linear: a binding budget costs about 25% of quantity almost immediately
design: Replication of E-195's cap sweep on the corrected population (post 4981384 and f37b702, pre 9331329), seeds 91-92, caps 1500-6000, 8h. Dose = per-role admitted-throughput deficit, response = filled-quantity loss.
finding: The linear model does not replicate. E-195's slope 0.836 with R2 0.989 and a near-zero intercept becomes 0.687 and 0.493 across two seeds, with a pooled intercept of +0.081 that survives seed averaging. The intercept is not noise: it is what fitting a line to a concave curve produces. Between zero and 15% deficit the loss reaches 25.3%, a local slope near 1.7; between 15% and 76% it only reaches 54.9%, a local slope near 0.48.
refines: E-195's claim of uniform sublinear harm with slope 0.836. That fit sampled no point between 0 and 6.8% deficit on one seed and mistook the average of a curve for a constant.
mechanism_hypothesis: A threshold rather than smooth concavity. Seed 92 at 8.5% deficit loses 23.9% and seed 91 at 21.6% loses 26.8%: a 2.5x difference in dose produces almost no difference in harm. This fits E-193's finding that binding budgets delay the start of the next parent rather than slowing the current one, which would cost a roughly fixed slice of throughput as soon as the budget binds at all.
caveats: Two seeds. The cap-2000 point has a 19.5 point spread between them, so individual points are not reliable even where the averaged curve is smooth.
No point sampled between 0 and 8.5% deficit, which is exactly where the threshold would sit. E-200 probes it.
Ran before the sub-minimum sizing fix (9331329), so the population still carried 44k invalid requests per run. Per-role metaorder counts are unaffected by that.
next: E-200 sweeps caps 6500-8000 on both seeds to locate the threshold, if it is one.

title: Admitted deficit is a mediator, not a dose; against the cap the response is monotone with a step
design: Probed caps 6500-8000 on seeds 91-92 to sample the 0-15% deficit region no earlier run reached, then re-expressed every point of E-195/E-197 against the cap instead of the admitted deficit.
finding: A tighter cap can produce a smaller admitted deficit: cap 7000 gives a 21.1% deficit and cap 6500 gives 6.3% on the same seed. Admitted deficit cannot be a dose because the desk's request demand is endogenous, so throttling changes the trajectory and therefore the denominator. Against the cap the response is monotone on both seeds, with a step between cap 7000 and 6500 (7.9% to 20.6%) larger than the whole 6000-to-3000 range.
supersedes: The dose variable used in E-191 through E-197. Those experiments regressed the response on a mediator; their slopes (0.836, 0.687, 0.493, 0.581) describe a relationship between two outcomes and should not be read as harm per unit of denial. The qualitative results those runs produced — harm appears as fewer parents started, execution quality is unaffected, the response is concave — are re-expressible against the cap and survive.
methodological_finding: This is the third dose variable this campaign has used: refusal rate (retry-inflated, E-190), admitted deficit (endogenous, here), and the cap itself. The pattern is that anything the agent's own behaviour can influence is not a treatment. Only the experimenter-set parameter is.
caveats: Two seeds; individual points still disagree by up to 19.5 points (E-197).
The step location is bracketed only between cap 7000 and 6500 and may be a smooth transition sampled coarsely.
Cap is orders_per_day per client while runs are 8h, so the cap's absolute scale is not directly the number of orders a desk may send in a run.
next: Bracket the step between caps 6500 and 7000 on more seeds, and re-derive the mechanism using TraderID (4071c66), since the between-parent timing claim in E-193 was measured on a merged record list and is currently unverified.

title: Throttling stretches the execution tail; it does not delay the next parent
design: Per-desk timing via TraderID (4071c66, tooling cd9eaad) on the current binary, seed 91, control and caps 7000/6750/6500, 8h. Seeds 92-93 still running.
finding: The gap between one parent ending and the next beginning is exactly 60 seconds in every arm, median mean and max alike: the rest interval is rigid and the budget does not touch it. Execution duration has a fixed 2.00s median and a mean that rises 89% from 17.89s to 33.83s as the cap tightens, with the p95 rising and the 900s MaxDuration ceiling present throughout. A cycle is duration plus rest, so a stretched execution tail is what reduces the number of parents that fit in the horizon. Parent loss at cap 6500 is 18.0%, matching the 18.6% quantity loss measured independently in E-200.
falsifies: E-193's mechanism claim that the budget does not stretch execution and instead delays the start of the next parent. Both halves are inverted. That claim was read from mean duration over filled parents on a merged record list, before TraderID existed; the effect lives in a tail that a median cannot see and the merged list corrupted.
survives: E-193's cost result. Median duration is unchanged at 2.00s and the slippage invariance was per filled parent, so throttling still does not degrade a typical execution.
caveats: One seed so far; seeds 92-93 pending in the same batch.
Zero-fill parents rise from 20 to 51, a small but monotone increase not yet accounted for.
The 900s maximum is the configured MaxDuration in every arm, so the tail is censored and the true stretching may be larger than the mean suggests.
next: Confirm on seeds 92-93, then test whether the stretch is child-level: children per parent against child inter-arrival time.

title: Rate-limit harm is a rare stall, not a slowdown: 2.9% of parents consume 27% of the horizon
design: Decomposed the E-201 duration rise on seed 91: children per parent, seconds per child, filled quantity per parent, and the count of parents reaching the 900s MaxDuration ceiling.
finding: Nothing about a normal execution changes under throttling: seconds per child is 1.81, 1.77, 1.82, 1.82 and filled quantity per parent is 0.35 in every arm. The entire duration effect is a stall count rising from 20 to 52 parents. Stalled parents run to the 900s MaxDuration ceiling having filled nothing — the stall counts match the zero-fill counts almost exactly — and each stall costs 900s plus 60s of rest, about 15 normal cycles. At cap 6500, 2.9% of parents consume 27.1% of the desks' combined horizon. The throughput loss is those stalls crowding out ordinary parents.
refines: E-201's framing of a stretched execution tail. The tail is not stretched; it is a distinct failure mode with a fixed 900s cost, and its frequency is what the cap controls.
explains: The step between cap 7000 and 6500 in E-200. Below some cap the budget runs dry inside a parent rather than between parents, and each such event costs a fixed fifteen cycles rather than a proportional slice.
mechanism_hypothesis: A parent whose children are refused makes no progress and sits until MaxDuration. This is untested: the stall's cause has not been traced to refusals in the event log, only inferred from its coincidence with the budget.
caveats: One seed; seeds 92-93 pending.

MaxDuration censors the stalls at 900s, so the cost per stall is a floor set by configuration rather than a measured quantity. A different MaxDuration would change the harm, which means the headline percentages are configuration-dependent.
Stall count and zero-fill count are close but not identical (52 against 51 at cap 6500); the discrepancy is unexplained.
next: Confirm on seeds 92-93, then trace a stalled parent in the event log to test whether refusals are the cause.

title: Parent loss equals horizon lost to stalls, one for one, across three seeds
design: Replicated E-202 on seeds 91-93 at caps 7000/6750/6500 against unbudgeted controls, then tested the mechanism quantitatively: regressed parent-count loss on the extra share of desk horizon consumed by stalled parents relative to each seed's own control. 6 desks x 8h of desk time is the denominator.
finding: Parent loss is the horizon lost to stalls, one for one. The slope of 1.164 is close to the value the mechanism predicts: a stall costs its own 900s plus the 60s rest that follows it, a ratio of 1.067. Stall counts rise monotonically with the cap on all three seeds. Effect size varies by a factor of three between seeds (18-19% parent loss at cap 6500 on seeds 91-92 against 5.8% on seed 93), but the accounting holds within 1.7 points at every point regardless.
establishes: The causal chain for FFA-99: a tighter cap raises the frequency of parents that stall to MaxDuration without filling; each stall consumes a fixed block of desk time; the throughput loss is those blocks crowding out ordinary parents. Rate of harm is set by stall frequency, and severity per stall is set by MaxDuration.
verification: Seed 93 gives identical parent and stall counts at caps 7000 and 6750, which the campaign's identical-result rule flags. Checked: admitted requests differ (28048 against 27548), so the runs are distinct and the coincidence is in the outcome, not a duplicated run.
caveats: MaxDuration is configuration, so cost per stall is a parameter rather than a measured property. The one-for-one accounting would hold at any setting, but the harm percentages would not.
The cause of a stall remains untraced. Coincidence with budget exhaustion is strong but no stalled parent has been followed through the event log.
Seed 93 shows the same mechanism at a third the magnitude, unexplained.
next: Trace one stalled parent through the event log to establish why it makes no progress.

title: Stalls are a pricing failure, not a refusal; and every unthrottled stall is a buy
design: Traced one stalled parent (trader 136, venue north, cap 6500, seed 91) through the event log, then tabulated stall side across seeds 91-93 for control and cap 6500.
finding: The stalled parent was never denied anything: 899 children submitted, 899 accepted, none refused, none filled. max_slippage_bps is unset in the reference configuration, so each child is priced exactly at the last seen touch and clamped to the size displayed there. The book moved about 0.03 per second and every child missed by roughly one tick for 900 seconds.
falsifies: The mechanism hypothesis recorded in E-202, that a parent whose children are refused makes no progress. For this parent the refusal count is zero.
unexplained: Parents are drawn 50/50 by side, but all 57 stalls across the three unthrottled control runs are buys. Throttling then introduces sell-side stalls that do not otherwise occur (12, 13 and 4). The buy and sell paths in executeChild look symmetric, so this asymmetry is not yet located.
preserves: The accounting in E-203 is unaffected: parent loss still equals horizon lost to stalls at slope 1.164 with R2 0.983. What changes is the cause of a stall, not its cost.
implication: The reference configuration leaves the metaorder desk unable to cross a moving book, which is the same at-touch pricing weakness measured in carry_arb (6.8% conversion) and round_trip (7.4%) in E-199. The code supports pricing through the touch and its own documentation warns that clamping to displayed size makes participation a property of maker quote size; the configuration does not use it.
caveats: One parent traced. The 899-accepted-zero-filled pattern has not been confirmed across other stalls.
Whether setting max_slippage_bps removes stalls is untested, and it would change the desk's market impact as well.
next: Test whether the buy-only asymmetry is a pricing or a balance effect, and whether a configured slippage allowance removes stalls without distorting the impact measurement.

title: Stalled buys had crossable liquidity every second, and unfilled IOC expiry is never logged
design: Followed the traced stalled parent (client 46, venue north, cap 6500, seed 91) second by second: compared each child's limit price against trade prices at the same timestamp, then audited how IOC orders terminate across the whole venue log.
finding: Every one of the 899 seconds in which a child was submitted also contained a trade at or below that child's own limit price, and no child filled. Separately, stalled buys occur in falling markets (median -7.1 bps local drift) where a buy priced at the last seen ask should fill more easily, not less. Both observations contradict the latency-race reading of E-204.
logging_gap: Unfilled IOC orders terminate silently. The venue logged 42915 IOC acceptances and not one cancellation carrying an IOC time in force, so an IOC that expires unfilled leaves no record of ending. Any analysis of IOC outcomes is blind to how they finish, which is why the stall looked like inactivity rather than repeated misses.
anomaly: A marketable IOC buy priced at or above available liquidity must fill. Either the liquidity visible in the trade log was not on the book at the instant the child was matched, which second-resolution sim_ts cannot distinguish, or the matching path is not crossing when it should. This is not yet attributable to the agent, the configuration, or the engine.
caveats: sim_ts has one-second resolution, so same-timestamp does not establish simultaneity. Intra-step ordering could explain the coincidence without any defect.
One parent traced in detail; the side asymmetry from E-204 (57 of 57 control stalls are buys) remains unexplained and may share this cause.
next: Write a direct test: submit an IOC buy at and above the resting best ask and assert it fills, to separate an engine defect from intra-step ordering. Log IOC expiry so the outcome of an IOC is observable at all.

title: The matching engine is not the cause: IOC crosses correctly on both sides
design: Direct engine tests (commit 57c24f1) submitting an IOC against resting liquidity at the touch, one tick through, and far through, on both sides, to discriminate an engine defect from intra-step ordering as the explanation for E-205.
finding: A marketable IOC crosses resting liquidity in every case tested, on both sides. The engine is not the cause of the stalls in E-205.
resolves: The E-205 anomaly in favour of the benign explanation. sim_ts has one-second resolution, so a child's arrival and the prints at or below its price are grouped into the same timestamp while the book moved between them. The desk prices at the last seen touch and the touch has moved by the time its order is matched.
remaining_puzzle: Why every stall in an unthrottled run is a buy (57 of 57 across three seeds) is still unexplained, and the direction is counterintuitive: stalled buys occur in falling markets (-7.1 bps median local drift), where a buy priced at the last seen ask should cross more easily rather than less. A simple race against requoting makers predicts the opposite side.
outstanding_defect: Unfilled IOC expiry is still unlogged (E-205): 42915 IOC acceptances and no corresponding termination event. Until that is logged, an IOC's outcome is only inferable from the absence of a fill.
caveats: The tests establish engine behaviour under direct submission, not under the simulation's phase ordering. They rule out a matching defect, not an ordering one.
The buy-only asymmetry may still indicate a defect somewhere in the agent or the phase schedule.
next: Log IOC termination, then use it to test the buy asymmetry directly rather than inferring it from stall counts.

title: IOC termination is now observable
design: TDD fix (commit ef5cfdf) for the logging gap found in E-205. A non-resting order that discards a remainder now logs an OrderCancelled event carrying remaining_qty and a reason.

tests: unfilled IOC against an empty book logs its full quantity as expired
partially filled IOC logs only the remainder
reason distinguishes IOC_EXPIRED from a market order's NO_LIQUIDITY

finding: An IOC that missed the touch previously left no trace at all, making it indistinguishable in the log from an agent that never submitted. That is precisely why the stalls in E-202 read as inactivity for two experiments before the trace in E-204 showed 899 submissions behind them.
implication: Every fill-conversion figure this campaign has reported was computed as fills over acceptances, with the denominator's fate unobservable. Those figures were not wrong, but the reason for a low conversion — missing the touch against resting unfilled — could not be distinguished until now. This bears directly on the 6.8% and 7.4% conversions for carry_arb and round_trip in E-199.
caveats: The event is emitted where the remainder is discarded, so it inherits that path's clock and ordering; it has not been checked against the gateway notification for duplication at the actor level.
Only spot IOC paths were exercised by the new tests.
next: Re-run control and cap 6500 on seeds 91-92 with expiry logged, then test the buy-only stall asymmetry directly against per-order outcomes instead of inferring it from stall counts.

title: Metaorder buys miss the touch 90% of the time; sells miss 2%
design: First use of the IOC expiry log (ef5cfdf). Joined each IOC acceptance to its termination by order id and tabulated the miss rate by side for metaorder_trader, seeds 91-92, control and cap 6500. Then tested two book-level explanations.
finding: Buy children miss the touch about 90% of the time and sell children about 2%, consistently across seeds and arms. The desk sends roughly eight times more buy orders than sell orders as a direct consequence: a sell parent completes in a few children while a buy parent grinds. This is the quantitative form of the 57-of-57 buy-only stall asymmetry from E-204.
explanations_ruled_out: Book asymmetry: median distance from mid is 0.42 on both sides.
Reprice frequency: the ask changes in 81.0% of snapshots against 74.1% for the bid, far too small a difference to produce 90% against 2%.
Matching engine: E-206 showed IOC crosses at, one tick through, and far through the touch on both sides.
open: The cause is unlocated. The buy and sell paths in executeChild differ only in which side of the touch is read and in the direction of tick rounding, and both round in the aggressive direction. Since the effect survives in carry_arb (96% miss) and round_trip (93% miss), both of which price at the touch with independent code, a shared cause outside the agents is more likely than three parallel agent bugs.
caveats: Two seeds, one venue examined for the book diagnostics.
Miss rate is measured per child, not per parent; a parent can miss many times and still complete.
next: Compare, for a sample of expired buys and filled sells, the submitted price against the book state at the matching instant rather than at snapshot time. That distinguishes a stale-view problem from a submission-price problem.

title: Stale views are symmetric, so they do not explain the buy-side miss rate
design: For every metaorder IOC on venue north (seed 91, control), compared the submitted price against the best quote in the snapshot at the same timestamp and in the following snapshot, by side. Also inspected the maker requote sequence for an ordering window.
finding: Every child of both sides is marketable against the book as published at its own timestamp, and staleness against the next snapshot is comparable between sides (74.4% against 82.7%). Buys nonetheless miss 88.2% and sells 1.7%. Orders that are marketable against both the current and the following book still expire, so a stale view cannot be the cause.
explanations_ruled_out: Book asymmetry in spread or reprice frequency (E-208).
Stale market-data view, ruled out here.
Maker requote ordering emptying the ask side: spot_maker_submit_before_cancel is true, so both the old and new asks rest simultaneously and the ask side never empties during a requote.
open: An IOC buy priced at or above the published best ask expires without filling, in a configuration where the engine's direct tests show it should cross. The difference between the passing test and the simulation is everything the phase schedule adds: intra-step ordering, several actors submitting within one step, and market data published at step boundaries.
caveats: One venue and one seed for the price comparison.
Snapshot timestamps have one-second resolution, so 'the book at its own timestamp' is the book as published for that second, not necessarily the book at the matching instant.
next: Reproduce inside the simulation runtime rather than against a bare exchange: one maker requoting each step and one at-touch IOC taker on each side, asserting symmetric fill rates. That is the smallest setting containing the phase schedule.

title: The buy-side miss rate is contention for the touch, not a defect
design: Two probes inside the deterministic phase runtime (commit 5ce62e3). First: one requoting maker whose mid walks between steps, plus one at-touch IOC taker per side. Second: the same with one added competitor that sweeps the whole displayed ask each step.
finding: With no competition an at-touch desk fills every order on both sides, so neither the phase schedule nor the engine has a side asymmetry. One competitor sweeping the displayed ask each step takes the buyer to zero while the seller is unaffected. This reproduces the 88-95% buy miss against 1.7-1.9% sell miss measured in reference runs, and the same pattern in carry_arb (96%) and round_trip (93%).
resolves: The anomaly chain from E-204 to E-209. Engine crossing (E-206), book symmetry and reprice frequency (E-208), stale views and maker requote ordering (E-209) were each ruled out; contention is the ingredient that only exists once the population is present.
mechanism: An order priced exactly at the touch and clamped to the displayed size can only fill if nothing scheduled ahead of it consumes that size first. The population's aggressive flow is buy-heavy at the touch, so the ask is repeatedly swept before the at-touch desks are scheduled while the bid survives.
implication: For metaorder_trader, carry_arb and round_trip as currently configured, fill rate measures queue position rather than strategy. Any comparison between these desks, or any measurement of how a rate limit affects them, is confounded by where each sits in the phase order relative to the flow that consumes the touch. This applies to the conversion figures in E-199 and to the stall frequencies underlying E-202 and E-203.
caveats: The probe uses one sweeper and one maker; it demonstrates the mechanism is sufficient, not that it accounts for the full 90% in the reference runs.
Which participants actually consume the ask in a reference run has not been attributed; noise_flow sends market orders and is the most likely candidate but this was not measured.
Nothing here is a defect to fix. Setting max_slippage_bps would let these desks cross, but it changes their market impact and is a design decision, not a correction.
next: Attribute the flow that consumes the touch in a reference run, then decide whether the reference configuration should give these desks a slippage allowance.

title: 98.5% of volume is maker against maker, and the requote order is why at-touch buys starve
design: Attributed every trade on ABC/USD (venue north, seed 91, control) to the roles owning the taker and maker order ids, by side and quantity.
finding: Five spot makers account for 98.5% of traded volume by crossing each other; every other participant combined is 1.5%. Aggressive flow is 82.9% sell. The requote submits the bid before the ask, so a fresh bid rests while the fresh ask crosses another maker's resting bid and executes on submission instead of resting. The book therefore carries bids and chronically thin asks, which starves an at-touch buy and leaves an at-touch sell unaffected.
falsifies: E-210's stated mechanism, that the population's aggressive flow is buy-heavy and sweeps the ask. The flow is sell-heavy. The runtime probe in E-210 remains valid as a demonstration that contention is sufficient to produce the asymmetry, but the contention in the reference run is not what that probe modelled.
corrects: E-209's dismissal of maker requote ordering. That reasoning assumed submit-before-cancel keeps the ask side populated because old and new asks rest simultaneously. It does not follow: the new ask never rests, because it crosses a bid on arrival.
implication: This is a campaign-level confound rather than a detail of one desk. Any statement about market behaviour in these runs is a statement about five makers churning against one another. Strategy desks are 1.5% of volume, so measurements of their fills, conversions and stall frequencies describe their position relative to that churn.
caveats: One venue, one seed, one configuration.

Whether the maker-versus-maker crossing is itself intended is a separate question; the campaign's earlier notes record cancel-then-replace lockstep quoting as a known collapse mechanism, and this configuration uses submit-before-cancel.
The mechanism linking requote order to the thin ask is inferred from the ordering and the 82.9% sell aggression, not yet demonstrated by a probe that reverses the submission order.
next: Probe whether submitting the ask before the bid reverses the asymmetry, which would confirm the ordering explanation and show the effect is an artifact of quote submission order rather than of strategy.

title: Quote submission order decides which side starves, confirming the E-211 mechanism
design: Runtime probe (commit f12891b) with two makers quoting overlapping prices so their quotes cross, plus one at-touch IOC taker per side. Ran once with the bid submitted first and once with the ask first.
finding: Reversing the order in which a maker submits its two quotes reverses which side of the book starves, from 20.6% buy against 100% sell to 100% buy against 0.5% sell. The leg submitted second crosses a resting quote and executes on arrival instead of resting, so that side of the book stays thin.
confirms: The mechanism proposed in E-211. The Stoikov maker submits its bid before its ask, which is why at-touch buys miss 88-95% and at-touch sells 1.7-1.9% in reference runs.
method_note: A first version of this probe reported no effect because its two makers were offset by less than the spread and never crossed. Overlapping quotes are the precondition; without them the submission order is irrelevant. The null was a property of the probe, not of the system.
implication: The side asymmetry is an artifact of maker implementation, not an ecological result. Combined with E-211's finding that 98.5% of volume is maker against maker, the reference population's book is shaped mainly by how five makers sequence their own quote replacements. Any per-side measurement of a taker in these runs inherits that artifact.
caveats: The probe uses two makers and a fixed overlap; the reference run has five makers whose overlap varies with their inventory and volatility estimates.
Whether makers should cross each other at all is a separate design question. This experiment explains which side suffers, not why the crossing happens.
No fix is proposed here. Submitting both legs atomically would remove the ordering bias but would not stop maker-versus-maker crossing.
next: Decide whether the reference population should prevent maker-versus-maker crossing, since that is 98.5% of volume and the ordering artifact is downstream of it.

title: Makers cross because inventory skew exceeds their quoted spread, not because they disagree on value
design: Measured, for spot makers only, the dispersion of their forward price, the per-second move of that forward, the quoted half-spread, and the share of maker-seconds with only one side quoted. Reference run e5_ctl_91, venue north.
finding: The four spot makers agree on forward price exactly, so crossing is not disagreement about value. Their forward moves 0.01 USD per second against a 0.205 USD half-spread, so drift cannot cross them either. What separates them is inventory skew: at 25 bps of the full limit, a maker long 86 ABC prices about 0.62 USD below one short 39 ABC, giving a reservation gap near 0.9 USD against a quoted spread of 0.41 USD. Opposite-inventory makers therefore quote through each other by construction, and 76.5% of maker-seconds have only one side resting because the second leg submitted crosses and executes rather than resting.
corrects: Two figures reported earlier in this session, a 4305 USD dispersion of maker mids and a 97.6% cross rate. Both were computed across the perp maker (forward 368) and the spot makers (forward 4910) together, so they measured the price difference between two instruments. Spot-only dispersion is zero. The 98.5% maker-versus-maker volume share in E-211 is unaffected: it was computed on the ABC-USD book alone.
implication: The dominance of maker-versus-maker volume is a calibration failure, not an ecological outcome. Skew per unit of inventory is roughly twice the full quoted spread, so any inventory imbalance between makers produces crossing quotes. Widening the spread, reducing the skew, or bounding inventory earlier would each break the loop; which is correct depends on what the reference population is meant to represent.
caveats: One venue, one seed, one snapshot for the per-maker reservation reconstruction.
The skew fraction was inferred from quoted prices rather than read directly; InventoryLimit is not in the config and its default was not confirmed.
Whether some maker-versus-maker crossing is desirable is a design question. The finding is about its magnitude, not its existence.
next: Sweep quoted spread against inventory skew and measure the maker-versus-maker share, to find where the population stops being dominated by its own makers.

title: Inventory skew alone decides whether the population is a market; the spread is irrelevant
design: Crossed the maker's minimum half-spread (1, 4, 12 ticks) with its inventory skew (25, 5, 1 bps) on def_control, seed 91, 8h. Measured maker-versus-maker volume share, one-sided maker-seconds, per-role fill conversion, IOC misses, price path and maker inventory.
finding: Widening the quoted spread twelvefold changes nothing: the maker-versus-maker share is 98.5%, 98.7% and 98.5% at 1, 4 and 12 ticks. Cutting the inventory skew from 25 to 5 bps takes it to 0.1%. Skew level decides it, not the skew-to-spread ratio. Every taker recovers at the lower setting: carry_arb converts 6.8% to 97.8%, round_trip 7.4% to 97.4%, metaorder 25.2% to 111%, and IOC misses fall by one to two orders of magnitude.
falsifies: FFA-100 as stated, that the ratio of skew to spread drives the dominance. The spread arm of the sweep is flat.
optimum: The response is non-monotone. At 25 bps makers cross each other and starve outside takers. At 1 bps inventory runs away, median -135 ABC and tenth percentile -303, which is the unbounded accumulation the maker's own documentation warns about. At 5 bps inventory sits at 0.7 median with a bounded range, price drifts 0.09% instead of -1.78%, and tick volatility is lowest.
implication: The 98.5% churn reported in E-211 was a single mis-calibrated parameter, not an emergent property. Every measurement of a strategy desk in this campaign was taken in a population whose depth was consumed by its own makers before outside participants were scheduled.
caveats: One seed, one venue, three skew values. The optimum is bracketed, not located.
Volume falls from 236890 to 17083 ABC; that is the churn being removed, but whether the remaining flow is adequate for the strategy comparisons has not been checked.
Skew 5 was not tested against the spread arm beyond 4 ticks.
next: Replicate at seeds 92-93, then re-run the rate-limit and dispersion results against the 2026-08-17 reference to see which survive a population whose makers are not eating the book.

title: With maker churn removed, the population is structurally short uninformed flow
design: Attributed aggressive volume and population payoff at skew 5 against skew 25, then reconstructed the carry desk's hedge from the change in its spot balance against its perp position.
finding: Removing the maker churn does not produce a balanced market: it exposes that the population has almost no uninformed flow. Aggressive volume becomes 89.3% carry arbitrage, and noise flow is 430 ABC in both configurations — unchanged in absolute terms, it only looked larger against a smaller total. Makers pay about 4.96M USD to arbitrageurs and receive 0.12M from noise, a ratio near 1:42, so spot makers lose 6.2M over eight hours. A real venue's makers are solvent because uninformed flow exceeds informed flow; here it is inverted by a factor of forty.
correction: An intermediate reading of this session claimed the carry desk was running unhedged, long 2100 ABC spot against a 102 ABC perp short. That compared its total spot balance against its perp position; 2000 ABC was starting inventory. The change is +100.17 spot against -102.17 perp, delta-neutral within 2 ABC. Its profit is ordinary arbitrage capture at the configured 2 bps entry and 1 bps exit over 76M USD of traded notional.
also_verified: The perpetual is not mispriced: median 5001.78 against spot 5003.47, a 3.4 bps basis.
Conservation holds: population sum -2.50M against 2.44M of fees, residual -64k.
implication: Maker inventory misbehaviour at skew 25 is downstream of insolvency. A maker being adversely selected forty times faster than it earns spread accumulates inventory it cannot recycle, which is what drives the reservation skew that made makers cross each other. Scaling uninformed flow is therefore not a cosmetic rebalancing; it is the condition under which market making is viable at all.
caveats: One seed, one venue for the payoff attribution.
Whether makers become solvent at a given noise level is untested; the 1:42 ratio states the gap, not the remedy.
noise_flow order size is mvBasePrecision/100 against a maker quote of 5 ABC and a carry lot of 2 ABC, so the scale mismatch is in the configuration rather than in the agent.
next: Sweep uninformed flow size and count until maker payoff turns non-negative, then re-check whether the higher skew settings remain pathological once makers are solvent.

title: Skewing makes a maker predictable: makers are solvent below 5 bps and adversely selected above it
design: Bracketed inventory skew at 1, 3, 5, 8, 12, 15 and 25 bps on seed 91, and replicated 5 bps on seeds 92-93. Measured maker-versus-maker share, one-sided maker-seconds, population payoff by class, and maker inventory.
finding: Maker-versus-maker crossing switches on between 8 and 12 bps, rising from 1.2% to 61.2%. Independently of that, maker profitability switches sign between 3 and 5 bps: makers earn 2.7M at 3 bps while the carry desk loses 4.2M, and lose 6.2M at 5 bps while the carry desk earns 4.7M. The sign flip is not caused by the churn, which is negligible at both settings.
mechanism_hypothesis: Skewing the reservation with inventory makes a maker predictable. A desk that can infer where the maker will quote next trades against it profitably; a maker that does not skew keeps its spread but carries the inventory. This is untested as a mechanism and is inferred from the sign flip.
corrects: E-214's conclusion that 5 bps is the working region. That judgement used churn and inventory centring only. Solvency was not measured, and 5 bps is exactly where makers flip from profitable to insolvent.
tradeoff: No tested setting is best on all three measures. 1 bps: makers profitable, inventory drifts to a -135 median. 3 bps: makers profitable, inventory median -23, churn 0.1%. 5 bps: inventory best centred at 0.7 but makers lose 6.2M. The reference generation is set to 3 bps because an insolvent maker eventually stops being a maker.
caveats: One seed for the bracket; only 5 bps was replicated across seeds.
Payoff is terminal mark-to-market, so a maker holding inventory at a favourable mark can look solvent without having earned it.
The predictability mechanism is a hypothesis, not a measurement. A direct test would compare the carry desk's entry timing against the maker's quote revisions.
next: Test the predictability hypothesis directly, and sweep uninformed flow at 3 bps to see whether more noise widens the solvent region.

title: No adverse selection at any skew, and the maker payoff attribution does not reconcile
design: Tested the predictability hypothesis from E-216 three ways: realised spread captured on passive maker fills, post-fill markout at 10/60/300s, and the cost of the maker's perpetual hedge. Then reconciled the population payoff against a single maker's account.
finding: Realised spread captured on passive fills falls monotonically with skew, from 0.38 bps at 1 bps of skew to 0.11 bps at 12, but stays positive everywhere. Post-fill markout is zero to three decimal places at every horizon for skew 1 through 8, so makers are not being adversely selected. The perpetual hedge costs 0.41 bps and about 8.7k USD at skew 5. None of these can produce a multi-million dollar loss.
falsifies: The predictability mechanism proposed in E-216. If the carry desk were trading against a maker whose next quote it could infer, the maker's post-fill markout would be negative and would worsen with skew. It is zero.
inconsistency: A single spot maker's account at venue north changes by roughly 30k USD over the run at skew 3 and 2k at skew 5, while population_payoff.py reports -517k per member for the same class. The two cannot both be right. Until this is reconciled the solvency flip reported in E-216 is not established, and the reference generation's move to 3 bps rests on it.
unaffected: The churn threshold between 8 and 12 bps (E-214, E-216), which is measured from trade attribution rather than payoff.
The taker recovery from 6.8% to 97.8% conversion, also measured from fills.
caveats: Capture and markout are measured at venue north only.
The reconciliation compares one maker account against a class total of twelve members across three venues; the discrepancy is a factor of seventeen per member, too large for that to explain it.
next: Reconcile population_payoff.py against per-account balance changes before any further use of its numbers.

title: The payoff tool is correct; the reconciliation failure was a units error, and the solvency flip holds
design: Reimplemented population_payoff.py's calculation independently and compared it against the tool, then examined the per-member distribution of maker results across the skew bracket.
finding: An independent reimplementation reproduces the tool exactly. The maker solvency flip between 3 and 5 bps is not an averaging artifact: the median member goes from +351,780 to -659,777 and the count of profitable makers falls from 10 of 12 to 2 of 12.
retracts: The inconsistency reported in E-217. USD_PRECISION is 100_000, and the account comparison there divided USD by 1e6 and mis-scaled the perpetual's unrealized PnL, turning a -291,852 account into an apparent -30,000. The tool was never wrong.
restores: E-216's solvency finding and the reference generation's 3 bps setting, both of which E-217 had put in doubt.
separate_correction: Every absolute price quoted in this session's analysis is a factor of ten low: USD_PRECISION is 100_000, so the spot asset trades near 50,000 USD rather than 5,000. Ratios, basis points and percentage results are unaffected because the divisor cancels.
still_unexplained: E-217's measurements survive: captured spread stays positive at every skew, post-fill markout is zero, and the hedge costs 0.41 bps. Those cannot produce the loss. The maker account that does lose shows most of it in perpetual unrealized PnL, so the candidate mechanism is now basis risk between the spot inventory and the perpetual hedge rather than anything in the spot quoting.
caveats: The basis-risk candidate rests on one account's decomposition and has not been measured across the class.
The tool marks terminal inventory, so a maker holding a hedged pair through a basis move books that as a loss whether or not it would realise it.
next: Decompose maker result into spot trading, perpetual trading and basis revaluation across the class, to test whether the flip is a hedging artifact rather than a trading outcome.

title: The spot maker earns nothing from market making; its entire result is the perpetual hedge
design: Decomposed each spot maker's active result into three parts across the skew bracket: the change in spot holdings valued at terminal marks plus cash (spot trading), the change in the perpetual wallet (realised perpetual result), and the unrealised PnL on open perpetual positions.
finding: Spot trading contributes between -306k and +18k at every setting, against class totals ranging from +2.7M to -46.3M. The maker's entire result, in both directions, is its perpetual hedge: realised perpetual result and unrealised position PnL. Market making on the spot book earns the maker essentially nothing.
explains: Why E-217's spot-side measurements all looked healthy. Captured spread is positive, markout is zero and hedge slippage is 0.41 bps because the spot quoting genuinely is well behaved. It is also irrelevant to the outcome, which is decided on the perpetual.
reframes: The solvency flip in E-216 is not a market-making result. It is the sign of a perpetual exposure that happens to correlate with the skew setting, because skew determines how much inventory the maker takes and therefore how large a hedge it carries.
open: Whether the hedge is failing to neutralise or is being marked through a basis move. A maker long spot and short an equal perpetual should show offsetting contributions; here the spot side is flat and the perpetual side carries everything, which suggests the hedge is sized against inventory deviation while the spot inventory itself barely moves.
caveats: Terminal marks; a position held through a basis move books that as result whether or not it would be realised.
The decomposition attributes by wallet, so a perpetual trade that offsets a spot trade appears as two separate contributions rather than one hedged pair.
One seed.
next: Test whether the maker's perpetual exposure is actually offsetting its spot inventory, by comparing hedge position against inventory over time rather than at the terminal instant.

title: The hedge tracks inventory exactly; the perpetual loss is realised through re-hedging, not a hedging failure
design: Compared each spot maker's inventory against its hedge position over the whole run from maker_state, across the skew bracket.
finding: Hedge position and inventory are perfectly anticorrelated at every setting, and residual net delta is under 0.7 ABC against inventory of 42 to 152 ABC. The maker is delta-neutral throughout.
falsifies: The hypothesis from E-219 that the perpetual leg had become a standalone directional position because the hedge was sized against a deviation that barely moved. It tracks exactly.
reinterpretation: The perpetual result is realised through the act of hedging rather than by carrying an exposure. The maker re-hedges continuously — 10486 perpetual trades at 5 bps — so each inventory excursion and reversion realises a perpetual round trip, while the spot inventory returns to flat and is marked only once at the end. A delta-neutral book can still bleed if one leg realises continuously and the other does not move.
open: Whether that bleed is an economically real cost of hedging a mean-reverting inventory against a trending instrument, or an artifact of the decomposition marking spot terminally while the perpetual realises continuously. The class total, which is not decomposed, still shows -6.2M at 5 bps, so at least part of it is real.
caveats: Correlation is computed across all spot makers pooled at one venue.
Delta neutrality in position units does not imply neutrality in value if spot and perpetual prices diverge; the basis was measured at 3.4 bps median, which bounds how much that can contribute.
One seed.
next: Measure realised PnL per hedge round trip directly, and test whether it scales with the number of inventory excursions rather than with the size of the exposure.

title: Hedging costs two orders of magnitude more than quoting earns, and it is realised, not marked
design: Summed realised perpetual PnL and fees for spot makers from the derivatives log across the skew bracket, and expressed it per unit hedged against the spread captured per unit quoted.
finding: Realised perpetual PnL equals the perpetual wallet change exactly and fees are zero, so the maker's hedging loss is realised rather than an effect of terminal marking. Per unit hedged it costs 8.8 to 43 basis points, against 0.11 to 0.38 basis points captured per unit quoted. Execution slippage on the hedge is 0.41 bps, so the cost is not paying through the touch; it is hedging after the spot fill, at a perpetual price that has already moved.
resolves: The question left open in E-220. The bleed is economically real. It is not an artifact of marking spot terminally while the perpetual realises continuously.
qualifies: E-216's solvency result. On a realised basis the maker loses at every skew setting tested. The positive class totals at 1 and 3 bps come from unrealised perpetual position gains of 2.69M and 3.16M, which are terminal marks on open positions rather than earned result. Makers are not profitable at 3 bps; they are less unprofitable, and holding an open perpetual position that happened to be marked favourably.
implication: Market making is not viable in this population for a reason upstream of everything measured so far. The maker earns a spread of well under a basis point and pays tens of basis points to neutralise the resulting inventory. No setting of the skew fixes that, because skew only changes how often the hedge is rebalanced.
caveats: The lag explanation is inferred from the size of the cost against measured slippage, not measured directly. A direct test would time each spot fill against its hedge.
One seed.
Whether the hedge band and cadence are calibrated sensibly has not been examined; HedgeBandQty and the quote interval both govern how often a hedge is triggered.
next: Measure the delay between a spot fill and its hedge, and the perpetual price move over that interval, to confirm lag as the cost and to see whether a tighter hedge cadence or a wider band reduces it.

title: The maker's realised hedging loss is not explained by execution, lag or exposure
design: Tested three candidate sources for the 8.8 to 43 bps per unit hedging cost measured in E-221: execution slippage against the perpetual mid, the perpetual price move over the delay between a spot fill and its hedge, and the carry implied by the maker's signed average hedge exposure against the perpetual's drift.
finding: Hedge execution costs 0.41 bps with no tail: the tenth and ninetieth percentiles are -0.44 and -0.41. The perpetual moves 0.36 to 5.78 bps over the hedge delay. The carry implied by average signed exposure against perpetual drift is +200 USD per maker at 5 bps. The realised loss at that setting is -5.9M. Together the three candidates account for under 5% of the cost.
suspicion: A realised loss with zero fees that is not explained by execution, timing or exposure points at the perpetual PnL accounting rather than at the maker's behaviour. Candidates are the entry price carried through partial closes, and realised PnL being computed against mark rather than against entry.
discriminating_test: An engine test that opens a perpetual position at a known price, closes it at another known price, and asserts the realised PnL, including the partial-close path. This is the same method that cleared the matching engine in E-206.
caveats: Carry is computed from the mean signed hedge against start-to-end drift, which ignores the path; a position that varies with price can realise more than that product.
Lag is measured to the next hedge fill by the same client, which may not be the hedge for that particular spot fill.
One venue for the lag and carry measurements.
next: Write the perpetual realised-PnL engine test before drawing any further conclusion about market-making viability, since E-221's claim that hedging is unaffordable rests on this number.

title: The perpetual is untethered: funding settles once per run, so the basis wanders hundreds of basis points
design: Ruled out the perpetual PnL accounting with a direct engine test, then measured the spot-perpetual basis over time across the skew bracket and inspected the funding mechanism.

result.engine_test: six cases pass: long and short, closed higher and lower, and both partial-close paths

finding: The perpetual realised-PnL accounting is correct, so the maker's hedging loss is real. Its source is the basis: the perpetual starts pinned to spot and wanders to between -1288 and +989 basis points by the end of a run, with a standard deviation of 50 to 495 bps. FundingIntervalSeconds defaults to 28800 and every run in this campaign is 28800 seconds long, so funding settles once at the boundary and never exerts a restoring force during the run.
explains: The maker's unexplained hedging cost in E-221 and E-222. A maker long spot and short the perpetual is short the basis, so an untethered basis is a direct P&L. The sign follows the drift, which is why makers profit at 1 and 3 bps of skew and lose at 5 and above.
The carry desk's 50M USD result in E-215. It is trading a basis that wanders freely rather than one that reverts.
invalidates: Any spot-perpetual basis result in this campaign, including E-221's conclusion that hedging costs two orders of magnitude more than quoting earns. That number measures an untethered instrument, not the cost of hedging.
secondary_finding: The carry desk enters at 2 bps of basis and did not close a gap that reached 988 bps, so its position limit or lot size binds long before the basis is arbitraged away. A tethering mechanism cannot be assumed to come from the arbitrageur.
caveats: One venue for the basis series.

Whether a shorter funding interval restores the tether is untested; real venues use eight-hour funding and rely on arbitrage to hold the peg between settlements, which is precisely what is not happening here.
The funding rate units were not verified; rates range -75 to 75 in unstated units.
next: Sweep the funding interval against the basis drift, and separately test whether the carry desk's limits prevent it from closing a wide basis.

title: Arbitrage capacity saturates before the basis closes: 3000 ABC cannot hold the peg
design: Compared each carry desk's terminal spot and perpetual legs against its configured MaxPosition, in the runs where the basis diverged.
finding: In every run where the basis diverged, the six carry desks are at exactly their combined 3000 ABC limit and the basis continues to widen past them, reaching 989 and -1288 basis points. The one run whose basis stayed near spot, at 77 bps, is the only one where the desks did not saturate. Arbitrage capital is exhausted before the peg is restored.
combines_with: E-223. The perpetual has no restoring force from funding, because the settlement interval equals the run length, and none from arbitrage, because the arbitrage is capacity-bounded at 3000 ABC against a population that keeps pushing. Neither mechanism that tethers a real perpetual is operating.
reframes: This is the carrying-capacity question the campaign asked earlier, answered concretely. The quantity that matters is not how many arbitrageurs exist but how much inventory they can hold: six desks at 500 ABC each is 150M USD of notional, and it is not enough to hold this peg.
caveats: MaxPosition defaults to 500 ABC and was never chosen deliberately for these runs.
Saturation is read at the terminal instant; a desk could saturate, unwind and resaturate without that being visible here.

Whether a larger cap closes the basis is untested and is the obvious next experiment, but capacity large enough to hold a peg against an untethered instrument may simply move the loss onto the arbitrageur.
next: Sweep carry capacity against basis divergence, alongside the funding-interval sweep already running, to see which of the two restores the tether and at what cost to whom.

title: Funding is economically inert: it transfers cash without moving the basis at all
design: Swept FundingIntervalSeconds over 300, 900, 3600 and 28800 at 3 bps of skew, seed 91, 8h. Measured the basis path, carry desk saturation and population payoff.
finding: The basis path is identical to one decimal place across a ninety-six-fold change in funding frequency, while payoffs move by tens of millions. Settling funding sixteen times more often transfers far more cash and changes no price. Funding in this simulation is a wealth transfer with no feedback into behaviour, because no participant's decisions depend on the funding rate or on the balances it moves.
falsifies: The funding arm of FFA-101. Shortening the interval to 300 seconds leaves the basis ending at 225.8 bps with a standard deviation of 65.1, unchanged. Funding is not the tether here.
identical_result_check: The campaign's rule treats identical results as a tooling failure. Here the price paths are identical by construction: the agents are not capital constrained and none reads the funding rate, so a cash transfer cannot alter their decisions. The payoffs differ across arms, which confirms the runs are genuinely distinct.
implication: A real perpetual is tethered because the funding rate is itself the arbitrage signal: paying to hold a position is what closes the basis. Here the carry desk trades the basis level and ignores funding entirely, so the mechanism that anchors a real perpetual is absent rather than mis-calibrated.
caveats: One seed, one skew setting.
Funding rate units were not verified; only its effect was measured.
This does not show funding is implemented wrongly. It shows nothing in the population responds to it.
next: E-226 sweeps carry capacity, the other candidate tether. If neither restores the basis, the perpetual needs a participant that trades the funding rate itself.

title: Capacity is not the tether either, and the basis divergence is a late-run event that follows option expiry
design: Swept carry MaxPosition over 500, 2000, 10000 and 50000 ABC per desk at 3 bps skew, seed 91. Measured basis, desk utilisation, execution and payoff, then profiled the basis through the run.
finding: Raising carry capacity a hundredfold changes the basis by 33 bps and leaves the desks using 1% of what they are allowed. They are not constrained by capital either: 176M USD of spot cash and 100M of perpetual margin go unused, and their orders fill at 100% conversion. They trade 88,043 ABC and end holding 3,089 because the basis oscillates across their entry and exit thresholds rather than staying wide.
falsifies: The capacity arm of FFA-101, and with the funding arm already falsified in E-224, the hypothesis as a whole. Neither candidate tether explains the divergence.
corrects: E-223's characterisation of the perpetual as untethered. Median absolute basis is 2.1 bps and the first three quarters of the run stay within about 5 bps. The divergence is a late-run event: 114 bps at 90% of the run, 229 bps at 99%, with only 18.5% of the run above 50 bps. The perpetual is tethered for most of its life and comes loose at the end.
new_lead: The divergence begins near minute 360, which is six hours into an eight-hour run. The option series in these runs expires at epoch 1735711203, exactly 21602 seconds after the start. The onset coincides with option expiry.
implication: The maker hedging losses in E-221 and E-222 and the carry desk's results are concentrated in the final fifth of each run rather than spread through it. Any per-run aggregate over these campaigns mixes a well-behaved market with a post-expiry dislocation.
caveats: Coincidence of timing is not causation; the expiry link is untested.
One venue, one seed for the profile.
The 33 bps difference between cap 500 and the larger caps is real but small, and the larger caps are identical to each other, which suggests a different constraint binds above 2000.
next: Test whether option expiry causes the divergence by running with the option book disabled, and by profiling dealer hedging around the expiry instant.

title: Option expiry causes the basis divergence: moving it moves the onset, removing it removes the effect
design: Three arms at 3 bps skew, seed 91, 8h. Baseline with a 6h long option and future tenor; a variant with both tenors moved to 4h; and a variant with the option book removed (option_dealer_count and option_flow_count set to zero) while retaining the 6h dated futures.
finding: Moving the option expiry from minute 360 to minute 240 moves the onset of divergence from minute 392 to minute 266, preserving a lag of about 30 minutes in both. Removing the option book removes the divergence entirely: the basis never exceeds 50 bps, peaks at 25.9 and ends at 2.2. The no-option arm retains dated futures expiring at the same 6h point, so the cause is the option book specifically rather than expiry in general.
establishes: Option expiry causes the spot-perpetual basis divergence. This satisfies both a dose-shift test, where moving the cause moves the effect by the same interval, and a removal test, where deleting the cause deletes the effect.
corrects_scope: The perpetual is well behaved in the absence of options: median absolute basis 1.6 bps, maximum 25.9 bps over an eight-hour run. Every claim in this campaign about an untethered perpetual, unaffordable hedging or outsized carry profits describes a market contaminated by a post-expiry dislocation in its final fifth.
affected: E-221's hedging cost of 8.8 to 43 bps per unit
E-223's untethered-perpetual characterisation, already partly corrected in E-226
the maker solvency flip in E-216, whose sign may follow the post-expiry drift rather than the skew setting
caveats: One seed per arm.
The 30-minute lag between expiry and onset is unexplained and may indicate the mechanism is a slow unwind rather than an instantaneous jump.
The mechanism itself is not identified: dealer delta collapsing at expiry is the obvious candidate but was not measured.
next: Profile option dealer hedging around the expiry instant to identify the mechanism, and decide whether the reference configuration should stagger expiries or extend the run so the post-expiry window is not a fifth of every measurement.

title: Option expiry leaves market makers unable to requote or hedge, and their stale quotes are then run over
design: Profiled participant behaviour around the expiry instant in the baseline run and in the no-option arm: order submissions, fills, cancels, rejects, perpetual hedging volume and maker internal state.

result.maker_state_after_freeze: still published every second, bid and ask still computed and drifting, one maker's inventory frozen at exactly 253.0 ABC from minute 380

finding: After option expiry the makers stop submitting new quotes and stop hedging on the perpetual, while continuing to fill 130 to 185 times a minute on quotes that already rest. There are no rejections, no errors and no rate-limit refusals. The maker still computes a bid and ask every tick and publishes its state, so the actor is running; it is the submission path that is blocked. In the no-option arm the same participants keep quoting and hedging at full rate through the end of the run.
mechanism: The Stoikov maker returns early from its quote cycle whenever len(mm.pending) is non-zero, which is also the path that triggers hedging. A request that is never acknowledged therefore blocks requoting and hedging permanently while resting orders continue to trade. This is the ghost-pending failure already recorded in this project for the randomwalk maker, where a forced cancellation that is not request-keyed leaves the actor's pending entry unresolved.
consequence: The basis divergence in E-227 is downstream of this. The perpetual is not being pushed away by expiry flow; it is left with only noise flow once the makers and the carry desk stop trading it, and the makers' stale spot quotes are simultaneously being run over.
caveats: The pending-map explanation is inferred from the guard and the observed behaviour, not from instrumented state.
Brief recoveries occur at minutes 386, 391, 392 and 393, so the block is not total for every maker; some clear and re-block.
One seed, one venue.
next: Reproduce in a runtime test: a maker quoting through an option expiry must keep requoting afterwards. Then trace which expiry-time notification leaves the pending entry unresolved.

title: Hedging is coupled to requoting, so a calm market leaves makers accumulating unhedged inventory
design: Traced the post-expiry stall to its cause: per-maker submission timelines, mark price publication, and per-minute spot price range in the baseline and no-option arms.
finding: All four makers stop submitting at the same minute, which rules out per-actor state. Mark prices keep publishing at 180 per minute in both arms. What changes is the spot market itself: after option expiry the per-minute price range halves to about 0.65 bps against 1.5 bps without options. The makers' computed quotes then round to the same ticks and the requote guard correctly suppresses resubmission. They keep filling 140 times a minute on the quotes already resting.
defect: hedgeDelta is invoked inside the requote cycle, after the guard that returns early when the quote is unchanged. A maker that has no reason to requote therefore also stops hedging, even though it is still being filled and its inventory is still moving. Quoting and hedging are two different obligations on two different clocks, and coupling them means a calm market silently disables risk management.
corrects: E-228, which attributed the stall to an unacknowledged request stuck in the maker's pending map. That is wrong: every maker resumes quoting later in the run, in matched bid and ask pairs, so nothing is permanently stuck. The ghost-pending pattern from this project's history fitted the symptom and was not the cause.
chain: Option expiry calms the spot market, the calm suppresses requoting, the suppression stops hedging, inventory accumulates unhedged, the perpetual is left to noise flow, and the basis diverges. The basis divergence measured in E-227 is four steps downstream of the expiry.
caveats: Why option expiry calms the spot market is not established.
One seed, one venue.
The coupling is a design choice rather than an obvious bug; a maker that quotes continuously would hedge continuously. It becomes a defect only because the requote guard exists.
next: Give hedging its own cadence independent of the requote decision, then re-run to see whether the basis divergence survives.

title: Decoupling the hedge from requoting makes the basis far worse, so the coupling is load-bearing
design: Wrote a failing test showing a maker with a requote threshold does not hedge when its quote is unchanged, moved hedgeDelta out of the requote cycle onto the maker's own tick, and re-ran the baseline and no-option arms.
finding: Hedging on every tick instead of only when requoting takes the median absolute basis from 2.1 to 830 bps and the maximum from 230 to 5330. The no-option arm, which was the well-behaved reference at 1.6 bps median, degrades to 760. The change is harmful everywhere, not only after expiry.
interpretation: The requote cycle was acting as the hedge's rate limiter. Freed of it, the maker hedges on every tick, and because each hedge is a marketable order into the perpetual, the maker's own hedging becomes the dominant flow and pushes the perpetual away from spot. The coupling identified in E-229 is real but load-bearing: it was doing a job nobody had written down.
revised_defect_statement: The defect is not that hedging is coupled to requoting. It is that the maker has no hedge cadence of its own, so whatever governs its quoting also governs its risk management. Removing the coupling without supplying a cadence replaces one failure with a worse one.
corrects: E-229's proposed fix, though not its diagnosis. Hedging does stop when requoting stops, and inventory does accumulate unhedged; the remedy proposed there is wrong.
caveats: One seed per arm.
A hedge cadence between every-tick and every-requote was not tested; the two endpoints bracket it.
The band and slippage settings were left at their reference values, and a wider band might make every-tick hedging harmless.
next: Give the hedge an explicit interval and band, sweep them, and find whether any setting both keeps inventory hedged through calm periods and leaves the basis intact.

title: A 60 second hedge cadence removes the basis divergence and halves maker inventory
design: Added MakerHedgeInterval so the hedge runs on its own timer, then swept it over 1s, 10s, 60s and 300s against the in-cycle behaviour, seed 91, 8h, with the option book present.
finding: At a 60 second cadence the basis never exceeds 20 bps over an eight-hour run with options present, against 230 bps in-cycle and 5813 bps at one second. That is tighter than the no-option reference arm, whose maximum was 25.9 bps, so the post-expiry divergence is removed rather than reduced. Median maker inventory falls from 104 to 28 ABC. The cost is residual net delta rising from 0.36 to 2.22 ABC, which is small against the 28 ABC of inventory it is managing.
resolves: The post-expiry basis divergence traced through E-227 to E-230. The chain was: option expiry calms the spot market, the calm suppresses requoting, and hedging stopped with it. Giving the hedge its own clock breaks the chain at the third link.
non_monotonic: The response is not monotone in the cadence. Both endpoints are bad for different reasons: too frequent and the maker's own hedges dominate the perpetual, too infrequent and inventory is carried unhedged between hedges. The interior is where both obligations are met.
caveats: One seed per cadence.
Only the interval was swept; HedgeBandQty and HedgeSlippageBps were left at reference values and interact with it.
The 300s arm has the lowest inventory but a 227 bps maximum basis, so inventory control alone does not predict basis behaviour.
Whether 60s remains right at other skew settings or population sizes is untested.
next: Re-run the earlier maker-economics measurements against the corrected reference, since E-216 through E-222 were all taken in runs whose final fifth contained this divergence.

title: With the hedge cadence fixed, maker results collapse by fifty times and market making is near breakeven
design: Re-ran the maker economics decomposition on the corrected 2026-08-17 reference, which uses a 60 second hedge cadence, at 3, 5 and 8 bps of skew, seeds 91 and 92.
finding: Maker class results fall from millions to tens of thousands: the largest magnitude across six runs is 142k against 46.3M before the fix. Market making is close to breakeven rather than catastrophically unprofitable. The spot contribution is now comparable to the perpetual contribution instead of being negligible beside it.
retracts: E-219's finding that the spot maker earns nothing from market making and that its entire result is the perpetual hedge. Spot contributes 44k against 21k of perpetual at 3 bps, so the earlier result was the basis divergence swamping a real spot P&L.

E-221's conclusion that hedging costs two orders of magnitude more than quoting earns, and the inference that market making is not viable in this population. Both were measured on runs whose final fifth carried the divergence.
qualifies: E-216's solvency flip. Makers are still worst at 5 bps on both seeds, but the differences are now tens of thousands rather than millions, and 8 bps is no longer clearly worse than 3. The ordering that motivated the reference generation's skew setting is much weaker than it appeared.
caveats: Two seeds per skew, and per-seed disagreement is large relative to the effect: 3 bps gives +81k and -5k.
These runs used log_mode none, so per-fill capture and hedging cost are not yet recomputed; that measurement is running.
Near breakeven is not the same as viable; a real maker needs to cover costs this simulation does not charge.
next: Recompute capture and hedging cost per unit on full logs, to replace the 0.27 bps against 28 bps comparison that E-221 drew from contaminated runs.

title: Hedging pays for itself at 3 bps of skew once it runs on its own cadence
design: Recomputed realised hedging PnL per unit hedged and captured spread per unit quoted on the corrected reference with a 60 second hedge cadence, seed 91, full logs, at 3 and 5 bps of skew.
finding: At 3 bps of skew the hedge now earns 0.51 bps per unit rather than costing 2.6, and at 5 bps it costs 2.37 rather than 28. Captured spread per unit quoted is unchanged at 0.32 and 0.23 bps. The improvement comes entirely from turnover: hedge volume falls from 26,760 and 42,271 ABC to about 8,000 in both arms. Hedging less often, not hedging better, is what closed the gap.
retracts: E-221's headline that hedging costs two orders of magnitude more than quoting earns. The true ratio on the corrected reference is roughly one to one at 3 bps, with the hedge slightly positive.
interpretation: The earlier cost was the maker repeatedly crossing the perpetual to chase an inventory that its own hedging was helping to move, during a period when the basis was diverging. Slowing the hedge both reduced the number of crossings and removed the maker's contribution to the divergence.
caveats: One seed per arm.
Capture is measured at one venue while hedging is summed across three, so the two are not directly summable into a P&L.
0.32 bps of capture on a 0.41 bps quoted spread still leaves market making marginal, and this simulation charges no maker costs beyond fees, which are zero here.
next: Re-run the campaign's earlier strategy comparisons against the corrected reference, starting with the rate-limit dose response, since those were measured under the same contamination.

title: Metaorder stalls vanish on the corrected reference
design: Compared metaorder parent outcomes on the contaminated reference against the corrected one, which uses a 60 second hedge cadence.
finding: No metaorder parent stalls on the corrected reference. Every parent fills, none reaches the 900 second horizon, and the buy-only asymmetry in stall sides disappears with them.
consequence: The stall phenomenon and everything built on it belongs to the broken population. E-202's account of harm as a rare catastrophic failure, E-203's conservation identity relating parent loss to horizon lost to stalls at R2 0.983, and E-204's finding that every unthrottled stall was a buy all describe a market whose makers stopped hedging after option expiry.
preserved: E-210 and E-212 remain valid as mechanism results. They were established in isolated runtime probes rather than in the reference population: an at-touch order starves when something ahead of it consumes the displayed size, and the maker's quote submission order decides which side that is. Those probes did not depend on the hedge cadence.
caveats: One seed compared so far; the budgeted arms are still running.
Zero stalls means the dose response must be re-derived from a different response variable, since parent loss through stalls was the mechanism.
Whether rate limits still harm this desk at all is now an open question rather than a settled one.
next: Complete the budgeted arms at caps 6500, 4500 and 3000 on two seeds and measure whether any harm remains once stalls are absent.

title: Rate-limit harm and its conservation identity survive on the corrected reference
design: Dose response on the corrected 2026-08-17 reference at caps 6500, 4500 and 3000 against an unbudgeted control, seeds 91 and 92, full logs. Measured admitted requests, parents, filled quantity, stalls, per-parent slippage, and the stall-horizon identity from E-203.
finding: On a population with no spontaneous stalls, a binding budget creates them: 69 and 13 stalls at cap 3000 where the control has none. Parent loss equals the horizon those stalls consume, at ratios of 1.06 and 1.25 against the 1.164 measured on the contaminated population. Per-parent slippage is unchanged at 0.31 to 0.34 bps across every arm, so execution quality is untouched.
restores: E-203's conservation identity, and with it the mechanism in E-202. Both were real properties of rate-limit harm. What was wrong was the baseline: the old population generated stalls for free through the hedge-cadence defect, so the measured stall counts mixed budget-induced and defect-induced stalls.
revises: The dose range. On the corrected reference the budget does not bind at all until cap 3000: caps 6500 and 4500 leave admitted requests and parents essentially unchanged. The earlier sweeps, which showed harm from cap 6000 upward, were measuring the defect's stalls responding to timing perturbations rather than a budget constraint.
caveats: Two seeds, and the same cap produces 38.1% and 8.5% parent loss because control demand differs by a third between them.
Only one binding cap was sampled, so the shape of the response between 4500 and 3000 is unknown.
E-193's result that execution quality is unaffected is confirmed here on clean runs.
next: Sample between caps 4500 and 3000 to recover the shape, then revisit whether the response is concave as E-197 claimed or simply a threshold at the point the budget binds.

title: On a clean population the response is a threshold followed by a straight line, not a concave curve
design: Sampled caps 4500, 4000, 3500, 3000, 2500 and 2000 on the corrected reference, seeds 91 and 92, and fitted parent loss against admitted deficit.
finding: Below the binding point the budget costs nothing: caps 4500 on seed 91 and 4000 on seed 92 leave parents essentially unchanged. Above it the response is close to linear in the admitted deficit, and the identity between parent loss and the horizon consumed by stalls holds at every sampled point with ratios between 1.03 and 1.25.
falsifies: E-197's concave dose response and E-200's step between caps 7000 and 6500. Both were shapes of the hedge-cadence defect. On a population without spontaneous stalls the only threshold is the point at which the budget actually binds, and past it the relationship is straight.
caveats: Seed 92 binds at a lower deficit than seed 91 for the same cap because its control demand is a third smaller, so the two seeds sample different parts of the range.
One point per seed and cap.
The cap-2000 arm on seed 92 had not finished when this was recorded.
next: Close FFA-99 with the corrected statement and move to the remaining campaign questions, which have all been measured on the contaminated population.

title: The triangular cross-rate is bounded, and the bound tightens on the corrected reference
design: Measured the deviation between the ABC/CDF cross-rate and the rate implied by ABC/USD and CDF/USD, second by second, on the contaminated and corrected references.
