finding: The cross-rate deviates from its implied value by a median 6.5 bps on the corrected reference against 10.4 on the contaminated one, and its ninetieth percentile of 17.5 bps sits just below the arbitrage desk's 20 bps entry threshold. Prices stay inside the band where arbitrage does not pay.
caveats: This is a bound, not a demonstration of causation; the desk's threshold and the observed p90 could coincide for other reasons.
One venue, one seed per arm.
The corrected reference charges no taker fee, so the desk's configured edge is the only cost-like barrier in play.
next: E-237 continues with edge thresholds of 5, 20 and 50 bps on two seeds. If the bound is set by the threshold, the deviation distribution should move with it.

title: The triangular bound is set by the arbitrageur's threshold plus execution friction, and the reference desk never trades
design: Swept the triangular desk's entry threshold over 5, 20 and 50 bps on the corrected reference, seeds 91 and 92, and measured the distribution of cross-rate deviation together with the desk's fill count.
finding: At a 5 bps threshold the desk trades 794 and 768 times and the maximum deviation is 17.5 bps on both seeds. At 20 and 50 bps it trades rarely or not at all and deviation reaches 28 to 38 bps. The bound moves with the threshold, so FFA-104's falsifier is not met.
refines: The bound is not the threshold itself. A 5 bps trigger produces a 17.5 bps maximum, so roughly 12 bps of execution friction sits between the signal and the correction: the desk must observe the deviation, submit three legs and have them fill before the opportunity moves.
config_finding: At the reference setting of 20 bps the desk records zero fills on seed 91 and 297 on seed 92 over eight hours. The triangular arbitrageur is effectively absent from the reference population, because its threshold sits above the deviation range the market produces. Any earlier campaign statement about triangular arbitrage in this configuration describes a desk that was not trading.
identical_result_check: Edge 20 and edge 50 on seed 91 produce identical deviation statistics. Both have zero fills, so the desk is inert in each and the two runs are the same market. The identity is expected rather than a tooling failure.
caveats: Two seeds, and seed 92 trades at 20 bps while seed 91 does not, so the threshold sits right at the edge of activity.
Deviation is measured from trade prices at one-second resolution, which mixes the three books' trading times.
No taker fee is charged, so the desk's threshold is the only barrier; with fees the floor would be the larger of the two.
next: Set the reference triangular threshold to a value where the desk actually trades, then re-examine whether the deviation bound tracks a real transaction cost rather than a configured trigger.

title: The triangular bound was a configured trigger, not a transaction cost
design: Held the desk's entry threshold at 5 bps and swept the venue's taker fee over 2, 5 and 10 bps, seeds 91 and 92. A three-leg loop pays three fees, so the predicted bound was 6, 15 and 30 bps.
finding: A fivefold change in transaction cost leaves the deviation distribution unchanged: the maximum is 17.5 bps at every fee, on both seeds. The desk's payoff falls from +3527 to -6522 USD across the same sweep, so it keeps trading the same opportunities and simply pays more for them. The bound was set by the configured trigger plus execution friction, and the transaction cost never entered.
corrects: E-238's reading, which took the 17.5 bps bound as evidence that arbitrage enforces a no-arbitrage condition. It enforces the desk's trigger. It also corrects a statement made earlier in this session that the corrected reference charges no taker fee: TakerFeeBps defaults to 5 when unset.
bears_on: The campaign's earlier result that cross-venue dispersion equals the round-trip transaction cost, with ratios 1.09, 1.01 and 1.07 at 4, 10 and 20 bps. That was measured with a different desk on the contaminated population and is not touched by this experiment, but the mechanism it claimed is exactly the one shown absent here, so it needs re-running before it can stand.
fix: Commit bcde26c requires the loop's gain to clear the configured edge plus one taker fee per leg, with the leg count and fee configurable and the scenario wiring the venue's own fee.
caveats: Two seeds per fee.
The fix is not yet measured; a re-run at the same three fees is in flight.
Execution friction of about 12 bps sits between trigger and bound regardless, so even a cost-aware desk will not hold the cross-rate to its cost.
next: Re-measure the deviation bound with the cost-aware desk. If the bound now moves with the fee, the no-arbitrage condition is economic rather than configured.

title: A cost-aware triangular desk abstains instead of losing money, and the bound follows the cost while it trades
design: Re-ran the taker fee sweep of 2, 5 and 10 bps after commit bcde26c made the desk require the configured edge plus one fee per leg, seeds 91 and 92.
finding: The desk earns 8202 USD at a 2 bps fee and abstains entirely above it, where its three-leg cost exceeds the deviation the market generates. It no longer loses 6522 USD trading opportunities that do not cover their cost. While the desk is active the bound reflects its total cost: a 2 bps fee with a 5 bps edge requires 11 bps and yields a 23.2 bps maximum, against 17.5 when the requirement was 5.
interpretation: Above a 5 bps fee there is no triangular arbitrage to do in this market, because the cross-rate rarely deviates by the 30 bps a round trip would cost. Abstention is the correct response and the observed bound is then a property of the market rather than of the desk.
caveats: Two seeds.
The bound at fee 5 and 10 on seed 91 is identical because the desk is inert in both, which the campaign's identical-result rule flags and which is expected here.
Execution friction still separates trigger from bound; the desk requires 11 bps and the deviation reaches 23.
next: None for FFA-104. The desk is cost-aware and the bound behaves economically.

title: Order size relative to quoted depth was what suppressed every stylized fact
design: Swept uninformed order size and its distribution against the 5 ABC maker quote: 0.01 ABC baseline, 0.5, 2.0, then 0.5 with Pareto tails at 1.5 and 1.2, and finally all mechanisms together. Seed 91, 8h, panel measured over the ABC/USD tape.
finding: Uninformed orders were 0.01 ABC against a 5 ABC quote, a ratio of five hundred to one, so every order was absorbed at the touch and the price moved only when a maker repriced. Raising the size and giving it a Pareto tail moves four of the six facts into their empirical ranges at once: the bid-ask bounce falls from -0.446 to -0.189, sign autocorrelation at lag one rises from 0.064 to 0.321, excess kurtosis goes from -0.60 to 40.9, and the Hill tail index falls from 39.5 to 3.43 against a canonical value near three.
falsifies: The arrival-process explanation in FFA-105. Self-excitation raised trade counts more than threefold and left the panel unchanged, because the excitation saturates at its cap of five and becomes a constant rate. Size, not arrival timing, was the binding constraint.
remaining_gaps: Volatility clustering is still absent: |return| autocorrelation stays near zero in every arm, where traded markets show 0.2 to 0.4 with slow decay.

Order-flow memory decays too fast. The 0.5 ABC arm reaches 0.163 at lag fifty, close to the empirical 0.2, but every heavy-tailed arm collapses to under 0.04: one large order replaces the run of same-signed orders that produces long memory in a real book, and the desks that would supply it by splitting are 1.5% of volume.
calibration: A 1.2 tail is too heavy, giving a tail index of 1.69 against an empirical 3. A 1.5 tail at 0.5 ABC is the closest arm tested.
caveats: One seed per arm.
The panel is measured on trade-by-trade returns, so the bounce dominates the first lag by construction.
Four of six facts in range is not a calibrated market; the two that fail are the ones that need a mechanism rather than a parameter.
next: Volatility clustering and flow memory both require a mechanism the population lacks: liquidity that withdraws under stress, and execution desks large enough for their splitting to shape the tape.
correction: Three of six, not four: sign ACF(1) moved from 0.064 to 0.321 but the empirical range is 0.5 to 0.8, so it moved in the right direction without arriving. The tail index of 3.43 is withdrawn entirely: the Hill estimate has no plateau on this sample (spread 1.31 across tail fractions from 0.01 to 0.20) and reading it at a hard-coded 0.05 produced a number for a sample with no power-law tail. At a 0.20 fraction the calibration reverses and Pareto(1.2) looks better than Pareto(1.5). Excess kurtosis is not an independent fact: it is not estimable when the tail index is below four, and 0.079% of the sample carried 70% of it.

title: Heavy-tailed order size buys realism at one horizon and destroys it at another
design: Adversarial audit of E-243 by a critique subagent, followed by a corrected panel: Hill estimates across tail fractions rather than at one, and returns resampled every 20 and 100 trades so they are comparable to the empirical values they are scored against. Also swept maker depth withdrawal under volatility at elasticities 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0.
finding: Resampling every hundred trades, return autocorrelation is +0.45 to +0.91 in every arm with larger orders, against -0.33 in the baseline. The price becomes strongly trending and predictable at that horizon, which is a worse departure from a traded market than the bounce the change was meant to fix. A large order walks the book and the price stays where it was pushed: nothing replenishes the consumed side or reverts the impact.
withdraws: The tail index reported in E-243. The Hill estimate has no plateau on any arm except Pareto(1.2), where it reads 2.65 with a spread of 0.67. On the reported arm the spread is 1.31 and the estimator is not measuring a tail.
also_falsifies: FFA-106. Withdrawing maker depth as volatility rises does not produce volatility clustering: the autocorrelation of absolute returns stays within 0.03 of zero at every elasticity tested, while the hundred-trade momentum stays above 0.75.
what_survives: The two seed-stable movements the critique confirmed at roughly twenty times the between-seed spread: the bid-ask bounce falling from -0.446 to -0.189 and sign autocorrelation at lag one rising from 0.064 to 0.321. Order size relative to quoted depth does govern price formation. It is the calibration built on top that does not stand.
caveats: One seed per arm; the critique measured between-seed spread on the tail index at up to 40% and on sign ACF(50) at a factor of two.
The strided panel is trade-strided, not wall-clock sampled, so it is closer to the empirical basis but not identical to it.
next: The missing mechanism is impact reversion: an uninformed order's push should decay as liquidity replenishes. Without it, larger orders trade a bounce artifact for a momentum artifact.

title: The hundred-trade momentum is an inventory-driven price collapse, not missing impact reversion
design: Cross-checked the strided autocorrelation with a variance-ratio test, which shares no machinery with it, then plotted the price path by decile and the maker inventory path by quartile.
finding: Every variance ratio is below one, so the price is mean reverting at every horizon, which contradicts the strongly positive strided autocorrelation. The contradiction resolves in the price path: the heavy-tail arms fall monotonically, 17.4% and 26.0% over eight hours, down in ten deciles out of ten, while the baseline is flat. The strided autocorrelation was reading a one-way drift, not stochastic momentum. Underneath that drift the microstructure mean reverts.
cause: Makers accumulate inventory in one direction and never shed it: a mean of +193 ABC and a terminal +1000 in the tail15 arm, against +2.7 mean in the baseline. Their inventory skew then drags quotes down for the whole run. Uninformed flow is symmetric by construction, so the asymmetry is in what the makers absorb, not in what arrives.
corrects: E-244's framing, which called this a momentum artifact and inferred that impact never reverts. Impact does revert; the price level does not, because nothing returns maker inventory to zero. The inference from a single autocorrelation was wrong and a second estimator caught it.
implication: The market has no mechanism that clears maker inventory. The skew is bounded at a few basis points at the inventory limit, which cannot attract enough offsetting flow to unwind a thousand-unit position, and the round-trip desk that would supply the other side is a fraction of volume. This is the same deficit measured in E-215 as a forty-to-one ratio of informed to uninformed flow, now visible as a price collapse rather than as a payoff.
caveats: One seed per arm for the path measurement.
The variance ratio and the autocorrelation disagree by construction under a drift; neither is wrong, but only the pair together identified it.
Whether the collapse would stabilise over a longer horizon is untested.
next: FFA-107 needs restating: the question is not impact reversion but inventory clearing. Test whether the index-anchoring sweep already running changes the drift, and whether an inventory-clearing counterparty removes it.

title: The market does have volatility clustering and fat tails; the panel was measuring in the wrong clock
design: Adversarial review by a microstructure critique subagent, which re-measured the reference tape independently and resampled it in calendar time rather than trade count. Then rebuilt the panel to report both clocks.
finding: Resampled at one second the reference arm shows an absolute-return autocorrelation of 0.441 with 0.199 still at lag ten, and an excess kurtosis of 31.6. Both sit inside the empirical ranges. In trade time the same tape gives -0.003 and -0.60. Absolute return in trade time is the pinned half-spread, so its autocorrelation is fixed by MinHalfSpreadTicks rather than by the price process, and the measurement reads zero whatever the market does.
retracts: Every statement in this campaign that the population has no volatility clustering, including the FFA-105 opening claim and the summary given to the user that the market lacks fat tails.
E-244's conclusion that maker depth withdrawal fails to produce clustering. It could not have been observed: the estimator was blind to it. The intervention's effect is unmeasured, not absent.
also_explains: Why self-excitation appeared to do nothing. Under a stochastic clock, clustering created by arrival intensity appears in calendar time and vanishes in trade time by construction, so measuring a Hawkes effect in trade time measures it in the coordinate system designed to remove it.
second_defect: The tape was ordered with an unstable sort while dozens of trades share one timestamp, so the differenced series was a permutation of the matcher's output. The bid-ask bounce figures were measured on it. Both defects fixed in 48c8caa.
remaining_real_gap: The sixty-second return autocorrelation of 0.888, which is the inventory-driven price drift measured in E-246, and long-lag order-flow memory at 0.038 against an empirical 0.2.
caveats: One seed per arm.
The one-second bucket is one choice of clock; the critique measured 1s, 10s, 60s and 300s and the clustering is strongest at 1s.
Kurtosis remains non-estimable as an independent fact when the tail is heavy.
next: E-247 tests the critique's structural claim: the population has no price-elastic demand of material size, so the price integrates order flow. elastic_supplier_units_per_percent has never been varied and the suppliers currently trade about 0.9% of volume.

title: Price-elastic demand removes the drift, at the cost of the fat tails
design: Swept elastic_supplier_units_per_percent over one, ten, a hundred and a thousand times its reference value on the heavy-tail arm, seed 91, 8h. The two largest arms also raise the supplier count from two to four.
finding: The eight-hour price excursion collapses monotonically from -17.4% to -0.02% as the elastic supplier's capacity rises, the correlation between maker inventory and the price level weakens from -0.844 to -0.178, and the hundred-trade variance ratio returns from 0.43 to 0.06. The drift is flow integration and a price-elastic counterparty removes it.
predictions_held: One-second clustering is unaffected: 0.441 to 0.390 across the sweep.
Long-lag sign autocorrelation is unaffected: 0.038 to 0.038. Elasticity does not address order splitting, as predicted.
predictions_failed: The sixty-second return autocorrelation does not fall monotonically: 0.888, 0.851, 0.357, 0.531. One seed per arm, so this may be noise, but it was predicted to be monotone.
The trade-time bounce was predicted to be unchanged and moved from -0.189 to -0.266.
cost: Excess kurtosis falls from 31.6 to 4.1, out of the empirical 5 to 50 band. The same mechanism that removes the drift removes the large excursions that produced the fat tails. A price pinned to its starting level is not more realistic than one that wanders.
caveats: The two largest arms change supplier count as well as elasticity, so the ablation is not single-variable and part of the effect may be the extra participants or the extra volume, which rose from 127k to 151k trades.
One seed per arm.
Whether the supplier is actually absorbing maker inventory, rather than the drift disappearing for another reason, is not yet verified from the logs.
next: A critique subagent is auditing the confound, the kurtosis cost and the mechanism. The single-variable run that would settle the first is elasticity at a hundred with the supplier count held at two.
correction: A single-variable control separates the two effects that were reported as one. Holding the supplier count at two and raising elasticity a hundredfold takes the eight-hour excursion from -17.4% to -0.4%, so elasticity does remove the level drift. It leaves the sixty-second return autocorrelation at 0.880 against the control 0.888. The fall to 0.357 came from raising the supplier count from two to four, not from elasticity. Seed 92 at count four gives 0.431, so seed noise on that statistic is around 0.07 and the count effect is outside it.
withdrawn_evidence: The correlation between maker inventory and price level is seed-unstable and cannot support the mechanism story: -0.634 at count two, -0.098 at count four seed 91, and +0.708 at count four seed 92. It changes sign.
audit_2026_08_18: A critique subagent reproduced every number and rejected the interpretation. The price change is an algebraic identity of the elastic supplier's own configuration: it holds a fixed ReferencePrice equal to the opening price, so the terminal price is -(excess supply)/capacity by construction, matching to three significant figures in six of six runs. That is a peg, not price-elastic demand, and it is an exogenous anchor of exactly the kind this campaign removed. Order-flow imbalance is invariant across every arm (total excess supply -10,410 to -10,189 ABC), so the treatment never touched the cause; it only moved which participant holds the imbalance. The recorded kurtosis cost is unsupported at n=2, where the two seeds give 4.60 and 9.03. The 60s autocorrelation spread in the low-drift regime is at least 0.17, three times the spread elsewhere, so the count-versus-persistence separation in E-249 is probably noise as well.

title: Elasticity fixes the price level; the number of independent suppliers fixes the persistence
design: Single-variable control for the E-248 confound: elasticity at a hundred times reference with the supplier count held at two, against the same elasticity with four suppliers, plus a second seed at four.
finding: Two effects were reported as one. Elasticity alone removes the level drift: the excursion falls from -17.4% to -0.4% with the supplier count held at two. It does not touch persistence, leaving the sixty-second autocorrelation at 0.880 against a control of 0.888. Doubling the number of suppliers takes that to 0.357 and 0.431 across two seeds, outside the roughly 0.07 seed spread.
interpretation: A single large elastic supplier anchors where the price ends up without changing how it gets there: its trades are correlated with themselves, so the path stays persistent. Several independent suppliers break that persistence because their demands arrive at different times. The level and the path are set by different properties of the counterparty population, capacity and independence.
withdrawn: The inventory-price correlation offered as mechanism evidence in E-248. It reads -0.634, -0.098 and +0.708 across the three arms and changes sign between seeds at identical settings, so it measures nothing stable.
caveats: One seed for the count-two arm.
Kurtosis still falls with elasticity, from 31.6 to 12.4 at count two and 4.6 at count four, so both levers cost tail weight.
A critique subagent is auditing this reading; its findings are not yet incorporated.

title: The price drift was underfunded uninformed flow, and the elastic supplier is an exogenous price anchor
design: Acted on an adversarial audit of FFA-108. Verified the supplier's reference price in code, measured order-side imbalance and rejection counts by role on the heavy-tail arm.

result.supplier_reference_price: mvBootstrapPrice, the opening price, hardcoded at sim.go:1430

finding: Uninformed traders held 100 USD while their orders grew to about 25,000 USD each, so only their buys were rejected and the population's random flow became 5.2% net short at 43 standard deviations. Makers absorbed that one-sided flow into inventory, and their skew priced the market down 17% over eight hours. The drift has a mundane cause upstream of everything FFA-108 proposed.
rule_violation: ElasticSupplier anchors to a fixed ReferencePrice equal to the opening price and trades against deviations from it forever. That is a permanent, privileged belief about the correct price, which is the exogenous fundamental this campaign was instructed to delete. It survived the purge because it is named elasticity rather than fundamental, and the FFA-108 sweep amplified it a thousandfold.
retracts: FFA-108's causal claim. The audit showed the price change equals minus excess supply over aggregate capacity to three significant figures in six of six runs, which is a clearing identity of the supplier's own configuration rather than a market mechanism.
fixes: Uninformed balances now scale with order size (noise_funding_lots, default 200 orders' worth).
Scan no longer treats an empty file selection as the whole run: a mistyped venue previously blended every book and reported 1.79 million trades for a venue that does not exist.
caveats: The funding fix is not yet measured; a re-run is needed to see whether the drift survives it.
triangle_arb is 42.5% one-sided at 323 standard deviations and is not yet explained.
option_dealer has 73,197 insufficient-balance rejections, an order of magnitude more than noise flow, and is unexamined.
next: Re-run the heavy-tail arm with funded uninformed flow at baseline elasticity. If the drift is gone, the elastic supplier was never needed and its exogenous anchor can be removed rather than calibrated.

title: Funding uninformed flow does not remove the drift, and the imbalance is in size rather than side
design: Re-ran the heavy-tail arm at baseline elasticity with uninformed balances scaled to two hundred orders' worth, seeds 91 and 92, and re-measured the side and quantity imbalance.
finding: Funding the uninformed traders for two hundred orders reduced their rejections by a quarter and left the drift and the imbalance untouched: the price still falls 19.2% and 18.0%, and the net position moves from -75,643 to -80,214 ABC. The falsifier for FFA-109 is met, so the balance asymmetry is not the cause as stated.
refines: The imbalance is not in side but in size. Fill counts are within 5% of even and the side is a fair coin by construction, while traded quantity differs by 9.5%: 378,885 ABC bought against 459,099 sold. A large buy requires far more quote currency than a large sell requires base, so the size tail is clipped asymmetrically at whatever balance the trader holds. Raising the balance moves the boundary without removing it.
caveats: Two seeds.
triangle_arb remains 42.5% one-sided by fill count at 325 standard deviations, though its net quantity is small at +8,880 ABC.
Whether the asymmetry survives at very large funding, or is a property of the Pareto draw interacting with any finite balance, is the next test.
next: E-252 continues with funding at two thousand and twenty thousand lots, and a uniform-size arm at high funding. If the imbalance persists at twenty thousand lots it is not a boundary effect; if the uniform arm is symmetric, the size tail is what interacts with the balance.
conclusion: Rejections reach zero at two thousand lots and the imbalance is unchanged, so it was never a balance effect. Removing the Pareto size tail at the same funding takes the imbalance from -3.8% to -0.1% and the price decline from -19.3% to -2.6%. The heavy size tail creates both. The asymmetry appears in filled quantity rather than in what is requested, so it is created during execution rather than in the order stream.
measurement_caveat: Filled quantity exceeds accepted quantity in both arms, 151.7% and 108.2%, so OrderAccepted under-records requests for market orders and the requested-versus-filled ratio cannot be used. Only the filled-side comparison is relied on here.
later_correction: The uniform and Pareto arms are not rate matched: a Pareto(1.5) draw has three times the mean of the uniform draw at the same interval, so the heavy-tail arm submits roughly three times the notional flow. Part of the -19.3% against -2.6% is volume rather than tail shape (E-254). The requested-side skew of -1.3% is also within one standard deviation and should not have been reported as a directional finding.

title: Maker inventory skew converts a small execution asymmetry into a price collapse
design: Single-variable separation at identical funding and zero rejections: Pareto(1.5) sizes with maker inventory skew at 3 bps and at 0, plus uniform sizes with skew at 0. Seed 91, 8h.
finding: Disabling maker inventory skew removes the price collapse entirely, from -19.3% to 0.0%, and cuts the traded imbalance from -3.8% to -1.2%. Heavy-tailed order sizes alone produce a small execution asymmetry of about -1.2% and no price movement. The skew is what turns it into a nineteen percent decline.
mechanism: Two stages. Heavy tails create a small net-selling asymmetry during execution, which is present with skew disabled and is the residual -1.2%. Maker inventory skew then closes a loop: absorbing net sales makes makers long, a long inventory lowers their quotes, lower quotes fill more sales, and the position grows. The skew is a control that becomes positive feedback once the flow it is controlling is itself asymmetric.
resolves: FFA-110's falsifier in the opposite direction to the one stated. The imbalance does not survive with skew disabled, so the cause is maker behaviour interacting with the size distribution, not the matching path alone. The residual -1.2% is the matching-path component and is not sufficient to move the price.
bears_on: E-214 and E-216, which tuned the skew on churn and solvency grounds without any measurement of its stability under asymmetric flow. The setting chosen there, 3 bps, is enough to produce a runaway decline once order sizes are heavy tailed.
caveats: One seed per arm.
Skew at zero removes inventory control entirely, which is not a usable configuration: it was a diagnostic, not a proposal.
The residual -1.2% execution asymmetry under heavy tails is unexplained; a bug hunt is running on it.
next: Find the skew level at which the loop is stable under heavy tails, and identify the residual execution asymmetry.

title: Unbounded market orders made executed flow conditional on book state
design: Bug hunt on the residual execution asymmetry, then a fix and a regression test. The hunt compared no-liquidity counts, early-versus-late asymmetry and a second instrument in the same runs.
finding: The taker sent market orders with no bound on visible depth, so executed quantity is the minimum of the drawn size and the depth facing it. The drawn side is a fair coin and the drawn size is independent of it, but the truncation is not: it falls on whichever side is thinner. With uniform sizes the bound never binds, 11 orders evaporate and flow stays symmetric. With a Pareto tail whose cap alone exceeds the entire visible book, 1557 evaporate and executed flow becomes conditioned on book state.
rules_out: Asymmetric reservation in the exchange. No code path reduces quantity by side, and the noise population had zero balance rejections on this book.
Price-level coupling. Sizes are base denominated and the falling price loosens the buy budget, the wrong sign.
Feedback as the origin. The asymmetry is present at the first noise tick before any price move, and is stronger early than late.
symmetry_breaking: The same run moved CDF/USD up 166% while ABC/USD fell 19.3%, with the same actors and seed. The direction is not a structural selling bias; the censor breaks symmetry in a random direction and maker inventory skew amplifies whichever way it broke.
confound_in_prior_work: The uniform and Pareto arms of E-252 were not rate matched. A Pareto(1.5) draw has mean three times the target while the uniform draw has mean equal to it, so the heavy-tail arm submitted roughly three times the notional flow at the same interval. Part of the -19.3% is a volume effect rather than a tail-shape effect, and the tail-shape claim needs a mean-matched arm.
significance_note: The requested-side skew of -1.3% is about one standard deviation at this sample size and is not significant. The -3.8% filled skew is.
fix: Commit 86ce326 bounds each order by the depth facing it, as every other taker in these scenarios already does, and stops the taker trading on its subscribing tick, which had it trading before any maker had quoted.
caveats: The fix is not yet measured against the drift.
Magnitude of the truncation channel was established by order counts and complete zero-fills; partial truncation was not summed.
next: Re-run the heavy-tail arm with the bound in place, and add a mean-matched uniform arm so the tail-shape claim is not confounded with flow volume.

title: Bounding orders fixes the flow imbalance but not the drift, and role-level net flow is unmeasurable from the fill log
design: Re-ran the heavy-tail arm with the depth clamp from 86ce326, plus a mean-matched pair: Pareto(1.5) at a third of the uniform target, since a Pareto(1.5) draw has three times the mean of a uniform draw at the same target.
finding: The clamp works on what it was aimed at: the uninformed imbalance goes from -3.8% to +0.4% at identical settings. The price still falls 17.9%, so the imbalance was not what drove the drift. Mean matched, the tail contributes about one percentage point (-3.1% against -2.0%), not the sixteen points attributed to it earlier.
corrects: E-252's central comparison. Most of the -19.3% against -2.6% gap was the unmatched flow volume of a Pareto draw whose mean is three times the uniform draw's, not the shape of the tail.
blocking_defect: Role-level net flow cannot be measured from the fill log. Summing signed fills across all roles on one book gives +191,776 ABC rather than zero, and separating by fill role gives 128,107 taker fills netting -13,925 against 128,107 maker fills netting +68,674. Each trade emits exactly one fill of each role, so if the maker record carried the maker's own side the two nets would cancel exactly. They do not.
invalidates: Every net-flow figure in this session that summed filled_qty, including the noise imbalances of -3.8% and +0.4% and the spot_maker net of +192,760 ABC. Percentages computed as a ratio of two filled_qty sums are less affected than absolute quantities, but both were wrong.
caveats: One seed per arm.
The clamp uses the last snapshot the taker received, so 965 orders still evaporate at the as-is settings; the bound is not tight.
The drift's cause is now unattributed: uninformed flow is symmetric and the participant-level accounting needed to find the seller is not trustworthy.
next: Establish the fill log's side convention for maker records before any further flow attribution. Until then use maker_state inventory, which is the actor's own accounting, rather than summed fills.
correction: The blocking defect was mine, not the engine's. OrderFill carries both qty, this execution's quantity, and filled_qty, the order's cumulative filled quantity. Summing filled_qty across an order's partial fills double counts it. Using qty, signed fills sum to exactly zero across roles and the maker and taker nets are equal and opposite at 37,897.7 ABC. The engine logs every trade once per side correctly.
corrected_finding: The clamp reduces the uninformed selling imbalance from -2.1% to -1.7% rather than removing it, so the earlier +0.4% was the same double-counting artifact. Uniform sizes are symmetric at +0.1% both before and after the fix, and a heavy tail leaves -1.3% to -2.1% net selling even bounded. Price change tracks maker net absorption across every arm: +5,600 with -19.3%, +5,020 with -17.9%, +1,799 with -3.1%, +1,599 with -2.6% and +665 with -2.0%.

title: Price change tracks maker net absorption across every arm tested
design: Recomputed all five arms with execution quantity after finding the double-counting error.
finding: Across five arms spanning two size distributions and the depth clamp, the eight-hour price change orders exactly with how much inventory the makers absorbed. Roughly 5,000 absorbed ABC accompanies an 18% decline and roughly 1,700 accompanies 3%.
caveats: Five points, one seed each, and the arms differ in more than one way.
Correlation across arms is not a mechanism: absorption and price move together and either could drive the other.
E-253 already showed that disabling maker skew removes the decline entirely, which favours absorption driving price through the skew rather than the reverse.
next: Test the relation directly by varying only how much the makers can absorb, through the inventory limit, at fixed flow.

title: At fixed flow, the price decline is set by the maker's inventory limit
design: Varied MakerInventoryLimit over 100, 500 and 5000 ABC on the depth-clamped heavy-tail arm, seed 91, 8h. Inventory enters the skew as a fraction of this limit clamped to one, so a larger limit means less skew per unit absorbed at the same flow.
finding: Uninformed net selling is near constant across the three arms at -2,933, -2,534 and -2,438 ABC, while the price decline collapses from 17.9% to 0.9%. The falsifier is not met: absorption through the inventory skew is the channel, and its strength is set by the limit rather than by the flow.
note_on_defaults: MakerInventoryLimit defaults to 100 ABC, not the 500 assumed while designing this sweep. The 100 arm therefore reproduces the earlier as-is run exactly at -17.9%, which is the consistency check that the two are the same configuration.
interpretation: The maker's own risk control sets how far the price moves for a given imbalance. A tight limit means the skew saturates early, so a modest absorbed position drags quotes the full configured distance and keeps dragging them. The population's price impact is a maker parameter, not a property of its order flow.
bears_on: E-214 and E-216, which chose the skew on churn and solvency grounds, and the reference generation which carries the 100 ABC default. Neither considered that the pair sets the market's impact coefficient.
caveats: One seed per arm.
Maker net absorption also falls with the limit, from 5,020 to 1,224 ABC, so the arms differ in absorption as well as in skew per unit. The two cannot be fully separated by this design.
The relation between limit and decline is monotone but the middle arm is much closer to the low-impact end than a linear reading would suggest.
next: Hold absorbed quantity fixed while varying the skew, which is the remaining way to separate how much is absorbed from how hard the quotes move for it.
